name: Gregory the Great

seo.title: Gregory the Great: the reluctant pope, his quotes and feast days
seo.description: Who Pope Gregory the Great was, in plain words: the monk made pope, the mission to England, the myths, his feast days East and West, and his own words.

band.lede: A monk made pope against his will, who fed Rome and sent the mission to the English.

picture.alt: Gregory the Great, an old bearded pope in a silver three-tiered crown and a white and gold cope, sits writing in a large book with a quill against a dark background
picture.credit: Saint Gregory the Great, Pope, Francisco de Goya, 1796-1799. Museo del Romanticismo, Madrid. Public domain.
picture.creator: Francisco de Goya

card.line: A monk made pope against his will, who fed Rome and sent the mission to the English.

filters.alias: pope gregory i gregorius magnus gregory the dialogist dialogus dvoeslov apostle of the english pastoral rule moralia dialogues

who: Gregory was a rich Roman who gave up the city's highest civil office to become a monk. In 590, a year of plague, Rome made him pope against his will. He fed the city, bargained with invaders and sent monks to the English. His handbook for pastors was read by bishops for centuries.

roles.name: Envoy
roles.line: At the emperor's court, about 579 to 586

lines: And six months and ten days
Six on his lands in Sicily
A seventh inside the walls of Rome
numbers.src: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1

lines: He bought them bedding for winter
To emperors, queens and farm managers

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 540, in **Rome**, to a rich senatorial family. His father was Gordianus and his mother Silvia.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: In Rome, in a family house on the Caelian Hill, while the Goths and the emperor's armies fought over the city. He was well schooled, but he never mastered Greek.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **12 March 604**, in Rome, after years of illness, above all gout. He was about 64.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: The same day, in the porch of St Peter's. His body now lies under an altar inside the basilica.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Pope Gregory I**. **Gregory the Dialogist** in the Orthodox Church, after his book of Dialogues. **The Apostle of the English**, after Bede. He called himself “servant of the servants of God”, and many of his letters open with it.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics and Orthodox, and one of the four great Doctors of the Latin Church. Anglicans and Lutherans keep his day too.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: Britannica lists teachers, students, singers, musicians, people with epilepsy, and **England**.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A pope in a tiara and full vestments, with a double cross. A dove is his special emblem. In Eastern icons he is a bishop, as in the icon on this page.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: The **Pastoral Rule**, a handbook for pastors. The **Moralia**, 35 books on Job. Four books of **Dialogues** on the holy men of Italy, with the only early life of St Benedict. Sermons on the Gospels and on Ezekiel. About 850 letters.

portrait.alt: A Greek icon of Gregory the Dialogist: a grey-bearded bishop in a gold crown and a white stole with black crosses raises his right hand and holds a long scroll of Greek writing, on a gold ground
portrait.credit: Icon of Saint Gregory the Dialogist, Cretan School, second half of the 17th century. Collection of Agia Aikaterini, Heraklion. CC0.
portrait.caption: A Cretan icon of the 17th century, from the monastery of Savvathiana. The East calls him Gregory the Dialogist. He holds a long scroll and raises his hand. Collection of Agia Aikaterini, Heraklion. CC0.

typeNote: The test itself is built on his Pastoral Rule. His Dialogues open with him alone in a solitary place, which he says suited “a sad and melancholy disposition”.

west.text: The **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **ELCA**. It was the **Catholic** feast too until 1969, and it is his day in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**.
**Catholic** memorial since 1969: the day he became pope, in 590. Also the **Church of England**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod**.

east.text: The **OCA**, the **Greek** churches and the **Russian Church**, as Gregory the Dialogist. The Russian Church keeps it on the old calendar, which is 25 March on today's calendar.

feasts.note: Why two dates? He died and was buried on 12 March, and Rome kept that day from the 8th century. But 12 March always falls in Lent. So in 1969 Rome moved him to 3 September, the day he became bishop of Rome. Churches on the old calendar keep 12 March 13 days later, on 25 March.

traits.title: homesick for quiet
traits.text: He loved the quiet life, and felt the busy one was forced on him. He compared himself to Jacob, who loved Rachel but was given Leah. “I have loved the beauty of the contemplative life as a Rachel, barren, but keen of sight and fair,” he wrote soon after he became pope.

cite.text: Letters, Book 1, letter 5, to Theoctista

traits.title: a dry wit
traits.text: He could be dry, even with emperors. Made pope against his will, he wrote that the emperor “has ordered an ape to be made a lion”. When the emperor Maurice called him simple, he answered that by that word “they politely call me silly”.

cite.text: Letters, Book 1, letter 5; Book 5, letter 40

traits.title: no grand titles
traits.text: When the patriarch of Alexandria called him Universal Pope, Gregory asked him to stop. “Away with words that inflate vanity and wound charity.” His honour, he said, was the honour of the whole Church and the strength of his brothers.

cite.text: Letters, Book 8, letter 30, to Eulogius

traits.title: patient until pushed
traits.text: He put up with a great deal, and then would not move. A man made bishop against the emperor's orders had Gregory's letters torn up in public. Gregory wrote to his envoy, “I bear long; but if once I have determined not to bear, I go gladly in the face of all dangers.”

cite.text: Letters, Book 4, letter 47

traits.title: open-handed
traits.text: He fed Rome from the Church's farms, paid ransoms for captives, and sent beds and cloaks as far as Mount Sinai. Bede says, “Whatsoever money he had, he took care to distribute diligently and give to the poor.”

cite.text: Bede, Book 2, chapter 1; Letters, Book 7, letter 26; Book 11, letter 1

traits.title: sick for most of his life
traits.text: He suffered from his stomach and from slow fevers, and later from gout. Late in life he wrote that for almost two years he had been “confined to my bed, afflicted with such pains of gout that I have hardly been able to rise on feast-days” to say Mass.

cite.text: Moralia, letter to Leander; Letters, Book 10, letter 35

said.lede: Gregory of Tours, a bishop in Gaul, wrote while he was alive. His own deacon was in Rome when Gregory was made pope. The English wrote of him a century later, as the man who sent them the faith.

quotes.q: And such was his abstinence in food, his sleeplessness in prayer, his determination in fasting that his stomach was weakened and he could scarcely stand upright.
quotes.who: Gregory of Tours, bishop and historian, on the new pope

cite.text: History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1

quotes.q: For we may rightly, nay, we must, call him our apostle.
quotes.who: Bede, the English monk and historian, about 731

cite.text: Ecclesiastical History, Book 2, chapter 1

quotes.q: Hunger and cold he overcame with food and raiment, and shielded souls from the enemy by his holy teaching.
quotes.who: His epitaph at St Peter's, as Bede copied it. It also calls him “Consul of God”.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 2, chapter 1

moments.title: The prefect becomes a monk
moments.text: By about 573 he was prefect of Rome, head of the city's government. Gregory of Tours says he used to wear silk robes and jewels. About a year later he gave it all up. He sold his goods for the poor, founded six monasteries on his lands in Sicily, and made his family house on the Caelian Hill into St Andrew's monastery. He admitted he had been slow to go: “for late and long I declined the grace of conversion”.

cite.text: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1; Moralia, letter to Leander

moments.title: Envoy to the emperor
moments.text: He was made a deacon, and Pope Pelagius II sent him as his envoy to the emperor's court. Some of his monks went with him, and his talks on Job to them became the Moralia. There he met Leander of Seville, who became a friend. He argued with the patriarch Eutychius, who taught that risen bodies could not be touched. Gregory pointed to the risen Christ, who said, “Handle Me and see.” The emperor took Gregory's side and had the patriarch's book burned.

cite.text: Moralia on Job, Book 14; Bede, Book 2, chapter 1

moments.title: The Angles in the market
moments.text: The English told this story about him. Bede says he saw boys for sale in the market in Rome, fair of skin and with beautiful hair. Told they were Angles, he said they had the faces of angels. He asked the pope to let him go to Britain himself. The Whitby Life says he set out, and on the third day a locust came to him as he read. He took its name as a message, {la|sta in loco}, “stay in the place”. Messengers soon caught up with him. The people of Rome had made the pope call him back.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 2, chapter 1; the Whitby Life, chapters 9 and 10

moments.title: Carried to St Peter's
moments.text: A deacon of Tours brought home the news. The Tiber had flooded Rome, and snakes were swept down the river, among them “a great serpent like a big log”. Then plague came, and it killed Pope Pelagius. Rome chose Gregory. He wrote to the emperor begging him to refuse, but the city prefect stopped the letter. He led the people in processions of prayer, and the deacon saw eighty fall dead in one hour. When Gregory was getting ready to hide, “he was seized and brought by force to the church of the blessed apostle Peter”. He was made pope on 3 September 590.

cite.text: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1

moments.title: A book for pastors
moments.text: In his first year as pope he wrote the Pastoral Rule, for John, bishop of Ravenna. It says who should lead, how a leader should live, and how to speak to each kind of person. Bishops used it as their handbook for centuries, and its third part is the base of our personality test. At the end he asks for prayers. He has drawn a good pastor, he says, without being one: “I have been as an ill-favoured painter pourtraying a handsome man”.

cite.text: Pastoral Rule, Part 4; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: Rome's defender
moments.text: The Lombards took town after town and came up to the walls of Rome, and the emperor's help was slow. So Gregory paid ransoms, fed refugees, named a commander on his own authority and bargained for peace, often against the emperor's wishes. Peace came in 599. Yet when he was accused of having a bishop killed, he answered that he had refused to have even Lombards killed: “since I fear God, I shrink from having anything to do with the death of any one.” Two centuries later Paul the Deacon quoted the letter, to show “how humble this man was and of how great innocence and holiness”.

cite.text: Letters, Book 4, letter 47; Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book 4, chapter 29; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: The mission to the English
moments.text: He sent Augustine, a monk of his own monastery, to the English with a party of monks. On the way they “were seized with craven terror”, says Bede, and sent Augustine back to ask to come home. Gregory wrote telling them to go on. They landed in Kent in 597. That Christmas, he told a friend, “more than ten thousand Angli are reported to have been baptized”.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 1, chapters 23 and 25; Letters, Book 8, letter 30

moments.title: Steps, not leaps
moments.text: At first he told King Ethelbert of Kent to pull down the pagan temples. Then he thought again. He sent word to Augustine through Abbot Mellitus: smash the idols, but keep the temples and make them churches. Let the people keep their feast days in a new form. For one who climbs “must needs rise by steps or paces, and not by leaps”. And when he heard of miracles in England, he warned Augustine not to let them make him proud.

cite.text: Letters, Book 11, letters 66, 76 and 28

miracles.lede: Gregory of Tours, writing in his lifetime, tells of his election with no wonders at all. The stories came later. The first are in a Life by a monk of Whitby in England, written early in the 700s. Paul the Deacon and John the Deacon added more. Gregory himself tells of wonders in his own monastery, like the one below. And in a book full of other men's miracles, he said what a life is judged by:

pledge.q: For true judgment of one's life is to be taken from his virtuous conversation, and not from the working of miracles.

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 1, chapter 12

items.title: Justus and the three gold coins
items.text: Gregory tells this one himself. Justus, a monk of his monastery and a doctor, had nursed him through his illnesses. Dying, Justus admitted he had hidden three gold coins, though the monks there owned nothing of their own. Gregory forbade the monks to comfort him, and had him buried in a dung heap with his coins. “Thirty days after his departure, I began to take compassion upon him.” He had Mass offered for Justus every day for thirty days. Then Justus appeared to his brother Copiosus.
items.quote: Hitherto have I been in bad case, but now I am well; for this day have I received the communion
items.witness: Copiosus, “who yet liveth”, says Gregory. The monks counted back, and it was the day of the thirtieth Mass.

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 4, chapter 55

more.title: The bread that bled
more.text: The Whitby writer calls this an old story. A Roman lady had baked the bread for Mass. When Gregory gave it to her as the Body of Christ, she smiled. He held it back and laid it on the altar. After Mass he asked her why she had smiled. She said she had made that bread with her own hands. He had the people pray, and on the altar the bread was found as a bleeding scrap, like a piece of a little finger. She believed. At their next prayer it became bread again, and she received it. Her words, in the Latin of the Life:
more.quote: Ego ipsos panes meis feci manibus

cite.text: Whitby Life, chapter 20, Gasquet's Latin edition

more.title: The dove at his lips
more.text: The Whitby writer heard that someone of Gregory's household saw a white dove sitting on him while he composed his sermons on Ezekiel. Gregory was angry, and forbade him to tell anyone while he lived. A later version, added to Paul the Deacon's Life, names the witness: Peter, his secretary. A curtain hung between them. When Gregory fell silent for long spells, Peter made a hole in it with his pen. This is why painters give Gregory a dove.
more.quote: he beheld a dove, whiter than snow, sitting upon Gregory's head, and holding its beak for a long time to his lips

cite.text: Whitby Life, chapter 26; Paul the Deacon, Life of Gregory, chapter 28, in Dudden's English

more.title: Tears for Trajan
more.text: The Whitby writer is careful with this one: some of his people, he says, heard it from the Romans. Crossing Trajan's Forum, Gregory remembered the pagan emperor Trajan, who once stopped on his way to war to do justice for a widow. Gregory went to St Peter's and wept for Trajan's soul, until he learned that his prayer was heard. He was warned never to ask it again for a pagan. The writer's own words:
more.quote: quidam quoque de nostris dicunt narratum a Romanis

cite.text: Whitby Life, chapter 29, Gasquet's Latin edition

more.title: The cloth that bled
more.text: Gregory told this story himself, of an earlier pope. Some Greeks doubted that cloths laid on martyrs' tombs were true relics. So Pope Leo cut one with scissors, and blood flowed from the cut. The Whitby Life later told a story like it of Gregory himself.
more.quote: the aforesaid pontiff took scissors and cut this same cloth (brandeum), and from the very incision blood flowed

cite.text: Letters, Book 4, letter 30, to the empress Constantina; Whitby Life, chapter 21

doubt.title: Doubted from the start
doubt.text: The Whitby writer says plainly what he had to go on: “we have only common report; we have not learnt orally from those who saw or heard”. Of the Trajan story, the English writer says the Romans told it, and the Roman John the Deacon says it is read in the English churches. Gasquet, who edited the Whitby Life in 1904, called it “harder to swallow in those days even than in these”.

words.note: His letters are in James Barmby's translation of 1895 to 1898, the Moralia in the Oxford translation of 1844, and the Dialogues in an English version of 1608. Where only his Latin is given, the English beside it is ours.

feature.q: It is, as it were, a kind of river, if I may so liken it, which is both shallow and deep, wherein both the lamb may find a footing, and the elephant float at large.
feature.ctx: Simple enough for a child, deep enough for the wisest. From the letter that opens his Moralia on Job. In Latin, {la|in quo et agnus ambulet, et elephas natet}.

cite.text: Moralia on Job, the letter to Leander

quotes.q: The government of souls is the art of arts!
quotes.who: Why no one should take charge of souls untrained.

cite.text: Pastoral Rule, Part 1, chapter 1

quotes.q: Holy Writ is set before the eyes of the mind like a kind of mirror, that we may see our inward face in it.

cite.text: Moralia on Job, Book 2

quotes.q: For I have lost the deep joys of my quiet, and seem to have risen outwardly while inwardly falling down.
quotes.who: Soon after he was made pope, to the emperor's sister.

cite.text: Letters, Book 1, letter 5, to Theoctista

quotes.q: By my exposition I have laid open my gifts, by my confession I discover my wounds.
quotes.who: The last page of his 35 books on Job.

cite.text: Moralia on Job, Book 35

quotes.q: For to adore a picture is one thing, but to learn through the story of a picture what is to be adored is another.
quotes.who: To a bishop who had smashed the pictures in his churches.

cite.text: Letters, Book 11, letter 13, to Serenus of Marseilles

quotes.who: Love itself is knowledge. On Jesus calling His disciples friends, in John 15. Our translation of his Latin.

cite.text: Homilies on the Gospels, Homily 27

myths.claim: Seeing fair English slave boys in Rome, he quipped *Not Angles, but angels*, in Latin {la|Non Angli sed angeli}.
myths.truth: The neat line is in neither early source. Bede has him say “for they have an angelic face, and it is meet that such should be co-heirs with the Angels in heaven”, and says the story came down “by the tradition of our ancestors”. The older Whitby Life makes the Angles visitors, not slaves, and has him say simply “Angels of God”. Gregory's own writings never tell the story.

cite.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History, Book 2, chapter 1; the Whitby Life, chapter 9; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: He wrote Gregorian chant, or gathered it.
myths.truth: The chant carries his name, but nothing in his own writings, his epitaph or the early Lives links him to it. The claim first appears in the 8th and 9th centuries. The historian Dudden wrote in 1905 that “the weight of evidence makes against the truth of the tradition”. Britannica still repeats it.

cite.text: Dudden, Gregory the Great, volume 1; Britannica, Gregorian chant

myths.claim: He drew up the seven deadly sins: pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, wrath and sloth.
myths.truth: His list is different. For him pride is not one of the seven but their root, “the queen of sins”. Her seven generals are “vain glory, envy, anger, melancholy, avarice, gluttony, lust”. Sloth is missing, and sadness stands in its place. The familiar list came later.

cite.text: Moralia on Job, Book 31

myths.claim: The Gregorian calendar is named after him.
myths.truth: It is named after a later pope, Gregory XIII, “who issued the papal bull Inter gravissimas in 1582”.

cite.text: Britannica, Gregorian calendar

myths.claim: Chosen pope, he escaped from Rome and hid in the woods for three days, until a pillar of light gave him away.
myths.truth: The story first appears in the Whitby Life. Gregory of Tours, whose own deacon was in Rome, says he was seized while “making ready to go to a hiding place”. The Catholic Encyclopedia says the flight to the forest “seems to be pure invention”.

cite.text: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book 10, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: During his plague procession, St Michael appeared on Hadrian's tomb, sheathing his sword, and the plague stopped.
myths.truth: The eyewitness account, from a deacon of Tours, has the procession but no angel. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls it a legend, and Britannica tells it as tradition. The legend gave the tomb its name, Castel Sant'Angelo.

cite.text: Gregory of Tours, Book 10, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia; Britannica

stood.lede: Each line is Gregory's own, from his books, sermons and letters.

learning.work: Letters, Book 11, letter 54, to Desiderius of Vienne

rulers.work: Letters, Book 11, letter 66, to King Ethelbert of Kent

extras.title: The hard parts
extras.lede: Some of what he wrote and did is hard to read today. Here it is plainly, in his own words and in his critics'.

items.title: The letter to Phocas
items.text: In 602 the soldier Phocas overthrew the emperor Maurice and had him and his sons killed. The next year Gregory wrote Phocas a joyful letter of welcome. The historian Gibbon said it “has sullied, with indelible disgrace, the character of the saint”. Defenders say Gregory may not have known how Phocas came to power, and that he honoured the office, not the man. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the question “a difficult one”.
items.quote: Glory to God in the highest Who, according as it is written, changes times, and transfers kingdoms

cite.text: Letters, Book 13, letter 31; Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 46; Catholic Encyclopedia

items.title: The Jews
items.text: He forbade forcing Jews to be baptised, and ordered that synagogues wrongly taken be paid for. Jews should have what the law allowed them, he held, no more and no less. But he also cut the rents of Jewish tenants on church land who became Christians, “to the end that others also, incited by this benefit, may be moved to a like desire”. Britannica sums it up: “His concern with justice for Jews was limited.”
items.quote: For, when any one is brought to the font of baptism, not by the sweetness of preaching, but by compulsion, he returns to his former superstition, and dies the worse from having been born again.

cite.text: Letters, Book 1, letter 47; Book 9, letter 55; Book 2, letter 32; Britannica

items.title: Pressure on pagans
items.text: Where preaching failed, he used pressure. He told a bishop in Sardinia to load pagan peasants on church land with heavy dues until they gave in. His own translator, James Barmby, wrote in 1895 that his zeal had betrayed him “into a certain human inconsistency”. Britannica adds that he advised Queen Brunhild to use armed force against pagans.
items.quote: he must be weighted with so great a burden of payment as to be compelled by the very pain of the exaction to hasten to the right way

cite.text: Letters, Book 4, letter 26, with Barmby's note; Britannica

items.title: Slavery
items.text: He freed two slaves of the Church, Montana and Thomas, and wrote that people are born free by nature. He also told his agent in Gaul to spend the Church's money there on clothes for the poor, or on English boys of about seventeen or eighteen “who may profit by being given to God in monasteries”. He ran the Church's great estates in an age of slavery, and never called for its end. Britannica says he “did tolerate slavery”.
items.quote: it is a salutary deed if men whom nature originally produced free, and whom the law of nations has subjected to the yoke of slavery, be restored by the benefit of manumission to the liberty in which they were born.

cite.text: Letters, Book 6, letters 12 and 7; Britannica

items.title: Mary Magdalene
items.text: In a sermon he made three women one. Luke's sinful woman, he said, is the Mary whom John names, and the Mary from whom Mark says seven demons were cast out. He called her a sinner, not a prostitute. In 1969 the Catholic calendar parted them again. Its day for her, 22 July, is for Mary Magdalene alone.

cite.text: Homilies on the Gospels, Homily 33; Calendarium Romanum, 1969

items.title: Pagan learning
items.text: He scolded Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, for teaching grammar from the pagan poets. A later tale says Gregory burned the Palatine library. Gibbon, no friend of popes, doubted it: “the evidence of his destructive rage is doubtful and recent”.
items.quote: we changed what had been said before into groaning and sadness, since the praises of Christ cannot find room in one mouth with the praises of Jupiter.

cite.text: Letters, Book 11, letter 54; Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chapter 45

items.title: Purgatory and hell
items.text: In the Dialogues he teaches a cleansing fire after death for small sins, and a hell that never ends. The Reformers rejected purgatory. Calvin called it “a deadly device of Satan”.
items.quote: But yet we must believe that before the day of judgment there is a Purgatory fire for certain small sins

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 4, chapters 39 and 44; Calvin, Institutes, Book 3, chapter 5

circle.name: Silvia
circle.text: His mother. After her husband died she took religious vows and lived apart in prayer, near St Paul's. Catholics keep her day on 3 November, and the OCA on 4 November.

cite.text: Britannica; Dudden, volume 1; Catholic Encyclopedia; OCA

circle.name: Tarsilla and Aemiliana
circle.text: His father's sisters. With a third sister they gave their lives to prayer. Gregory tells how Tarsilla, before she died, saw an ancestor of theirs, Pope Felix, in a vision.

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 4, chapter 16; Catholic Encyclopedia

circle.name: Peter the Deacon
circle.text: His deacon and secretary. Gregory says he had “always loved most entirely” since Peter was young. The Dialogues are written as talks between them.

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 1, preface

circle.name: Benedict of Nursia
circle.text: Gregory never met him. He wrote the only early life of Benedict, the second book of his Dialogues, from what four of Benedict's monks told him.

cite.text: Dialogues, Book 2, preface

circle.name: Leander of Seville
circle.text: Bishop of Seville. They met in Constantinople, and Gregory sent him the Moralia. When Leander wrote of his gout, Gregory answered that he too was “grievously worn down” by it.

cite.text: Moralia, letter to Leander; Letters, Book 9, letter 121

circle.name: Augustine of Canterbury
circle.text: A monk of Gregory's own monastery in Rome. Gregory sent him to the English, and he became their first bishop.

cite.text: Letters, Book 8, letter 30; Bede, Book 1

circle.name: Theodelinda
circle.text: The Catholic queen of the Lombards, wife of King Agilulf. Gregory sent her his Dialogues, and worked through her for peace.

cite.text: Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, Book 4, chapter 5; Letters, Book 14, letter 12

circle.name: The emperor Maurice
circle.text: Gregory stood godfather to his son. But they clashed over the Lombards and over church titles, and Gregory's letters to him are blunt.

cite.text: Gregory of Tours, Book 10, chapter 1; Letters, Book 5, letter 40

circle.name: John the Faster
circle.text: Patriarch of Constantinople, who took the title Ecumenical Patriarch. Gregory fought the title for years. After John died, he told the emperor that whoever calls himself universal priest “is in his elation the precursor of Antichrist”.

cite.text: Letters, Book 7, letter 33, to the emperor Maurice

death.big: He died in Rome on 12 March 604, after years of gout, and was buried the same day at St Peter's.
paras: For his last years he was mostly in bed. His letters speak of pain, and of longing for the end: “every day I faint under my sufferings, and sigh in expectation of the relief of death.”

In December 603 he wrote to Queen Theodelinda that gout left him hardly able to rise, “not only for dictating, but even for speaking”. Her envoys, he said, had left him “in the utmost peril and danger of our life”.
No one recorded his last words. The monk of Whitby, writing a century later, admits it: “Of the death of this man, how and of what manner it was, we have not heard.”

later.title: A later story
later.text: Famine followed his death, and his successor Sabinian stopped Gregory's free grain for the poor. Paul the Deacon's Life says Gregory appeared to him three times and gently urged him to be generous. The fourth time he rebuked him and struck him on the head, and Sabinian soon died. The historian Dudden says such stories “are not sufficiently well attested to be accepted as sober history”.

cite.text: Paul the Deacon, Life of Gregory, chapter 29; Dudden, Gregory the Great, volume 2

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and Anglicans count him a saint, and Lutherans remember him too. He was hailed a saint as soon as he died.

churches.note: One of the four great Latin Doctors. Memorial on 3 September
Church of England, 3 September. Episcopal Church, 12 March

paras: There was no formal canonization. The Catholic Encyclopedia says, “His canonization by popular acclamation followed at once on his death.”
Catholics count him one of the four great Doctors of the Latin Church, with Ambrose, Augustine and Jerome. In 1298 Pope Boniface VIII ordered the feasts of all four kept across the whole Church.
The Orthodox honour him warmly, though he was a pope of Rome. They call him the Dialogist, and credit him with the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, served on weekdays in Lent.

Calvin, the Protestant reformer, both praised and attacked him. He called Gregory “the last Bishop of Rome”, meaning the last true one. He also said Gregory was “most grievously and perniciously in error” in teaching that we can know we are called, but not that we are chosen.

quotes.q: At Rome, the raising to the Sovereign Pontificate of St. Gregory the Great, an incomparable man, who, being forced to take that burden upon himself, sent forth from the more exalted throne brighter rays of sanctity upon the world.

kin.name: Elijah
kin.text: After his great victory on Carmel he ran into the wilderness and sat under a tree. “I have had enough, LORD,” he said. The desert fathers remembered him as the one who “loved silence”.

kin.name: Monica
kin.text: Young Augustine loved friends, jokes and talk. He calls it “a restless youthfulness”. His mother Monica wept and prayed for him for years. A bishop told her, “it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.” Years later the two of them stood alone at a window in Ostia and talked together about God.
